essential: Paragraphs 1 and 2: Adams haunts the 1900 Exposition helplessly. Langley strips it to its forces, discarding the art and industrial exhibits. Langley's lesson is Bacon's: science is the economy of forces. Adams's business concerns forces since he began the study at Chicago in 1893. Keep the ironic note on 'ignorance' accumulated as inert facts. The Daimler motor and the automobile are measured against the steam-engine, which is Adams's own age.

The hall of dynamos: to Langley, the dynamo is a channel for the heat of coal. To Adams it is a symbol of infinity and a moral force 'as the early Christians felt the Cross'. Keep the wheel that 'would not wake the baby'.
The break of continuity between steam and electricity, like that between the Cross and the cathedral. Langley calls the new forces anarchical and 'parricidal', and 'Radium denied its God'.
Paragraph 5: the 'Paradise of ignorance'. The new forces have no common scale with the old and are measurable only by collisions. Keep 'physics stark mad in metaphysics'.

The historian's confession: sequence of men, society, time and thought fails, and his dozen volumes do not satisfy him. He turns to the sequence of force. The 1900 revolution is compared with 1500 and 1600, and most nearly with 310 and Constantine's Cross. The rays are 'immediate modes of the divine substance'.

Method: measure forces by their attraction on his own mind. Keep the Boston chemist who 'never heard of Venus except by way of scandal'. Keep the knife-edge 'like Sir Lancelot' between two kingdoms of force.

The Woman as once-supreme force, still felt in France and at Lourdes, but unknown or shamed in America. Keep the fig-leaves, and 'sex was sin' set against 'sex was strength'. The Lucretius and Dante invocations must be paired (Venus with the Virgin). Keep 'he read the letter, but he never felt the law'.

Paragraph 15: American art is sexless, with the exceptions of Whitman and Bret Harte. The historian stays neutral on the moral issue: 'He cared nothing for the sex of the dynamo until he could measure its energy.'

St. Gaudens: inarticulate and selfless, with poor health that summer. Keep the visit to Amiens and Gibbon's 'contemptuous look' as humor with real relation. Keep 'One sees what one brings', glossed as Gibbon bringing the Revolution and Ruskin the reaction. St. Gaudens loves the monuments but is unconscious of the force (the Isis comparison may be condensed).

St. Gaudens as a Renaissance survival and 'child of Benvenuto Cellini, smothered in an American cradle'. Each man had half a nature. St. Gaudens chose the horse of the Sherman monument as his symbol of power. Adams has felt the Virgin as force only since 1895, and only at Chartres, Lourdes and perhaps Cnidos.

Paragraph 21 argument: both energies act on man as interchangeable force. Mathematicians accept any useful symbol. The historian's business is to track the energy, and he 'rather inclined to think the Virgin easiest to handle'. Keep it hedged.

Paragraph 22: pursuit into scholastic science. Forty-five years were futile for power. Keep the pen as 'blind-man's dog' and the crystallization of form, and 'more on what is struck out than on what is left in'. Sailing from Cherbourg on January 19, 1901.
optional: Paragraph 2: the electric tram and locomotive comparison details can be condensed.

Paragraph 5: Marconi, Branly coherer, frozen air and electric furnace can be reduced to one example. Keep 'Branly coherer' if paragraph 14 ('as though he were a Branly coherer') is kept; otherwise drop both together.
Paragraph 13: the Dante tercet can be cut only if paragraph 12's 'Virgin of the Schools' sentence is rephrased to name Dante's invocation without quoting it.
Paragraph 16: the list of exuberant artists (Hunts, Richardson, La Farge, White) and the Whistler aside.
Paragraph 18: the Isis at Edfoo line.
Paragraph 20: Matthew Arnold at the Grande Chartreuse and the Indian goddesses.

title: THE DYNAMO AND THE VIRGIN (1900)
voice_profile: Adams narrates his own life in the third person ('the young man', 'Adams', 'one'), as an elderly, ironic observer judging a younger self he calls ignorant. His sentences are long and balanced, built from semicolon catalogues and paired antitheses ('grew smaller as it doubled in size; cheaper as it quadrupled its wealth'). He uses aphoristic reversals and deadpan self-deprecation. Every experience is measured against an ideal of 'education' and found a failure, or useful only by accident. Scientific and mechanical metaphors (force, dynamo, lines of force, mathematics) are applied to history, art and religion. He hedges with 'perhaps', 'possibly' and 'one might', and distinguishes what he felt then from what he concluded later.
book_context: The book is an autobiography in 35 chapters. A recurring device declares each stage a failed 'education' and introduces 'accidental education' as its by-product. Chapter V (Berlin) is the first self-directed attempt: Civil Law in Germany, prompted by Lowell. It sets up later motifs: the 'ghost of the Civil Law', accidental education, Marx and the Black District, Beethoven and Wagner, the State as a 'dynamo' polarizing minds, and Sumner as boyhood hero. Chapter XXV (Dynamo and Virgin) is the hinge of the late philosophical chapters. It picks up the Chicago 1893 study of force, Langley as guide, Gibbon at Ara Coeli, and St. Gaudens's Rock Creek figure. It leads into the Virgin-as-force of later chapters, the Thirteenth-Century Unity versus Twentieth-Century Multiplicity scheme, and the dynamic theory.
